name: Microservices Design Patterns

beginner.content:
The Problem

In a microservices architecture, one business application is broken into many small services - Order Service, Payment Service, Inventory Service, User Service, and so on.

If a mobile app or web client had to call each of these services directly, it would need to know the address of every single service, handle authentication for each one separately, and make many round trips over the network just to render one screen. This makes the client heavy, slow, and tightly coupled to the internal structure of the backend.

Real-Life Analogy


• Think of a big office building with 20 different departments (HR, Finance, IT, Legal).
• Instead of a visitor wandering the building looking for each department, there is a reception desk at the entrance.
• The receptionist routes the visitor to the correct department, checks their ID first, and keeps a log of who visited.
• The API Gateway is exactly this receptionist for your microservices.

Simple Explanation

Instead of clients calling every microservice directly, all requests go through a single entry point called the API Gateway. The gateway then routes the request to the correct backend service.

          Mobile / Web Client
                  |
                  v  (single entry point)
             API Gateway
        (auth, routing, rate limiting)
             /     |      \
            v       v       v
       Order   Payment  Inventory
      Service  Service   Service

What the Gateway Typically Handles


• Routing - forwards /orders/** to Order Service, /payments/** to Payment Service.
• Authentication / Authorization - validates a JWT token once at the edge.
• Rate Limiting - prevents one client from overwhelming backend services.
• Logging / Monitoring - one place to see all incoming traffic.

Basic Config Example (Spring Cloud Gateway)

A simple route says "any request starting with /orders should go to the Order Service." This is a configuration snippet (YAML), not a runnable Java program, so there's no console output to show.
codeExamples:
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: order-service-route
          uri: http://localhost:8081
          predicates:
            - Path=/orders/**
        - id: payment-service-route
          uri: http://localhost:8082
          predicates:
            - Path=/payments/**

expert.content:
Failure Scenarios It Handles


• Client-service coupling explosion - without a gateway, every client (web, iOS, Android, partner API) must know the network location of every microservice. Any service being renamed, split, or moved breaks every client.
• Cross-cutting concerns duplicated everywhere - without a gateway, auth, logging, and rate limiting logic gets copy-pasted into every microservice.
• Chatty clients over slow networks - a mobile client on a weak network making 6 separate calls to render one screen is far slower than one aggregated call to the gateway.
• Uncontrolled traffic spikes - a malicious or buggy client can hammer a single backend service directly if there is no central choke point to apply rate limits.

Architecture with Cross-Cutting Concerns (Illustrative Java Config)

This is a Spring Cloud Gateway Java-config route builder - illustrative of real production code, not something with a deterministic console output since it defines routing behavior for live HTTP traffic.

API Gateway vs Backend For Frontend (BFF)

AspectAPI GatewayBFF
PurposeSingle generic entry point for all clientsDedicated gateway per client type
Response ShapeUsually same shape for all clientsTailored per client (web vs mobile)
OwnershipOwned by a central platform teamOften owned by the frontend team
Best FitUniform clients, simple routing needsVery different clients with different data needs

Mitigating the Single-Point-of-Failure Risk

Because every request passes through it, the API Gateway can become a bottleneck if not designed carefully:
• Horizontal scaling - run multiple gateway instances behind a load balancer, never a single node.
• Statelessness - keep the gateway stateless so any instance can handle any request.
• Circuit breakers, timeouts, and bulkheads - isolate a failing/slow downstream service so it doesn't take down the whole gateway.
Real tools: Spring Cloud Gateway, Kong, AWS API Gateway, NGINX/Envoy.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why not let clients call microservices directly?Tight coupling, duplicated cross-cutting logic, and chatty network calls from weak client connections
What does an API Gateway typically handle?Routing, auth, rate limiting, logging, and request aggregation
How do you avoid the gateway being a single point of failure?Scale horizontally, keep it stateless, and use circuit breakers/health checks
API Gateway vs Load Balancer?A load balancer only distributes traffic; a gateway also does routing, auth, and transformation
API Gateway vs BFF?Gateway is generic and shared; BFF is tailored per client type
Which Spring project implements an API Gateway?Spring Cloud Gateway

beginner.content:
The Problem

In a microservices system, service instances come and go constantly - they scale up/down, crash and restart, or get redeployed with a new IP address. Hardcoding http://192.168.1.5:8081 for the Order Service into every caller breaks the moment that instance moves.

What is Service Discovery?


• A mechanism that lets services find each other's current network location dynamically, without hardcoded addresses.
• A Service Registry (e.g. Eureka, Consul) keeps a live list of "service name -> healthy instance addresses."
• Each service instance registers itself on startup and sends periodic heartbeats; instances that stop heartbeating are removed.

Client-Side vs Server-Side Discovery


• Client-Side Discovery - the calling service queries the registry itself, picks a healthy instance (often with load-balancing logic), and calls it directly. Netflix Eureka + Spring Cloud LoadBalancer works this way.
• Server-Side Discovery - the caller sends the request to a fixed address (e.g. a load balancer or the API Gateway), and that intermediary looks up the registry and forwards the request. AWS ELB + ECS service discovery is an example.

expert.content:
Registry High Availability and Self-Preservation

The registry itself must not be a single point of failure - Eureka servers replicate their registry to each other, so any Eureka node can answer lookups even if another node goes down.

Eureka also has a self-preservation mode: if it sees too many instances failing to heartbeat at once (often a network partition, not real instance death), it stops evicting them - preferring stale-but-present data over incorrectly wiping the whole registry.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why can't you just hardcode IP addresses between microservices?Instances scale, crash, and redeploy constantly, so a hardcoded address goes stale almost immediately
Client-side vs server-side discovery?Client-side: caller queries the registry and picks an instance itself. Server-side: caller hits a fixed address and an intermediary does the lookup/forwarding
What is a heartbeat used for in service discovery?Instances periodically ping the registry to prove they're alive; missed heartbeats trigger eviction from the registry
What is Eureka's self-preservation mode?It stops evicting instances if too many heartbeats are missed at once, to avoid wiping the registry during a network partition rather than a real outage
Name two real service discovery toolsNetflix Eureka, HashiCorp Consul (Kubernetes' built-in DNS-based discovery is another common example)

beginner.content:
The Problem

If Service A calls a struggling Service B repeatedly, and each call takes 30 seconds to time out, Service A's own threads/resources get tied up waiting - and if many callers do this, the failure cascades across the whole system, even though only one service was actually unhealthy.

What is a Circuit Breaker?

Just like an electrical circuit breaker trips to stop current flow when there's a fault, a software Circuit Breaker "trips" to stop calls to a failing dependency, failing fast instead of waiting on a doomed call and giving the failing service room to recover.

The Three States


• Closed - normal operation, calls pass through; the breaker counts failures.
• Open - once failures cross a threshold, the breaker "opens" and calls fail immediately (or return a fallback) without even attempting the real call, for a configured wait duration.
• Half-Open - after the wait duration, the breaker allows a small number of trial calls through; if they succeed, it closes again, if they fail, it re-opens.

CLOSED --(failure threshold hit)--> OPEN
   ^                                    |
   |                          (wait duration elapses)
   |                                    v
   +----(trial calls succeed)---- HALF-OPEN
                                        |
                              (trial calls fail)
                                        v
                                      OPEN
Resilience4j Circuit Breaker Example

expert.content:
Sliding Window and Failure Rate Threshold

Resilience4j doesn't count "last N failures ever" - it uses a sliding window (count-based or time-based) of the most recent calls, and opens the circuit once the failure rate within that window crosses the configured threshold (e.g. 50%). This avoids permanently tripping the breaker over one old failure that's no longer representative of the service's current health.

Circuit Breaker vs Retry - They Work Against Each Other Naively

Combining Retry and Circuit Breaker carelessly can backfire: if Retry keeps re-attempting a call that Circuit Breaker is trying to stop, you get MORE load on a struggling service, not less. The correct order is: Circuit Breaker wraps the Retry (or the breaker sits "outside" so once it's open, retries don't even get attempted) - most resilience libraries let you compose them explicitly in a defined order for exactly this reason.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does the Circuit Breaker pattern solve?Cascading failures caused by callers repeatedly waiting on/retrying a struggling downstream dependency
Name the three circuit breaker statesClosed (normal), Open (fail fast), Half-Open (trial calls to test recovery)
What triggers a transition from Closed to Open?The failure rate within the sliding window crosses the configured threshold
What happens during Half-Open?A limited number of trial calls are allowed through; success closes the circuit again, failure re-opens it
Why can combining Retry and Circuit Breaker backfire?Naive retries against an already-struggling service add more load; they must be composed so the breaker can stop retries once open
Name a Java library that implements thisResilience4j (Netflix Hystrix is the older, now-legacy equivalent)

beginner.content:
What is the Retry Pattern?

Many failures in distributed systems are transient - a momentary network blip, a service instance restarting, a brief spike in load. The Retry pattern automatically re-attempts a failed operation instead of failing immediately, on the assumption that the problem may already be gone by the next attempt.

Why Backoff Matters

Retrying instantly and repeatedly (a "retry storm") can make things WORSE - it adds more load onto an already-struggling service right when it needs relief. The standard fix is exponential backoff: wait longer between each successive retry (e.g. 200ms, 400ms, 800ms...), often with a small random "jitter" added so many clients don't all retry in perfect lockstep.
Resilience4j Retry Example

expert.content:
When Retry Helps vs When It Makes Things Worse


• Helps: transient network glitches, a load balancer momentarily routing to a not-yet-ready instance, brief GC pauses.
• Hurts: retrying a non-idempotent operation (e.g. "charge the card") can duplicate the side effect if the first attempt actually succeeded but the response was lost - retries should generally be limited to idempotent operations, or the operation should be made idempotent first (see the separate Idempotency pattern topic).
• Hurts: retrying against a service that's failing because it's overloaded adds MORE load, worsening the outage - this is why Retry is almost always paired with a Circuit Breaker that eventually stops the retries altogether.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What kind of failures does Retry help with?Transient failures - brief blips likely to have resolved by the next attempt
What is a "retry storm" and how do you avoid it?Many clients retrying instantly and repeatedly, worsening an outage; avoided via exponential backoff plus jitter
Why is retrying a non-idempotent operation risky?If the original call actually succeeded but the response was lost, a retry can duplicate the side effect (e.g. double-charging)
Why pair Retry with a Circuit Breaker?So retries eventually stop entirely once a dependency is clearly unhealthy, instead of continuing to add load

beginner.content:
What is the Timeout Pattern?

A Timeout bounds how long a caller will wait for a response from a dependency before giving up and moving on (often to a fallback or an error). Without a timeout, a single slow dependency can hold a caller's thread/connection indefinitely, and that pileup can cascade into resource exhaustion across the whole call chain.

Setting a Sensible Timeout

Too short: healthy-but-momentarily-slow calls get killed unnecessarily. Too long: the caller stays stuck for ages before giving up. A common practice is basing the timeout on the dependency's normal p99 latency plus some margin, not an arbitrary round number.

expert.content:
Timeout Budgets Across a Call Chain

In a chain A -> B -> C -> D, each hop needs its OWN timeout, and they should be set so the sum doesn't exceed the caller's own deadline. If A's overall budget is 5 seconds but B, C, and D each independently allow up to 5 seconds, a slow D can still blow A's entire budget. Distributed tracing/deadline-propagation helps enforce a shrinking "time remaining" budget as a request flows deeper into the call chain.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is an unbounded call dangerous in a distributed system?It can hold the caller's thread/connection indefinitely, and that pileup cascades into resource exhaustion up the call chain
How do you choose a timeout value?Base it on the dependency's typical p99 latency plus margin, not an arbitrary guess
What's the risk of chained timeouts in a multi-hop call?Each hop's independent timeout can sum to more than the original caller's overall deadline unless budgets are propagated/shrunk down the chain

beginner.content:
The Problem

If one service calls three downstream dependencies (Inventory, Payment, Shipping) using a SHARED thread pool, and Inventory starts responding very slowly, all the threads in that shared pool can end up stuck waiting on Inventory - leaving none available to handle Payment or Shipping calls either, even though those two dependencies are perfectly healthy.

What is the Bulkhead Pattern?

Named after a ship's bulkheads - watertight compartments that stop one flooded section from sinking the whole ship. The software version isolates resources (thread pools, connection pools) per dependency, so one failing dependency can only exhaust ITS OWN allotted resources, not everyone else's.
Resilience4j Bulkhead Example

expert.content:
Semaphore Bulkhead vs Thread-Pool Bulkhead


• Semaphore-based - limits the number of CONCURRENT calls allowed through using the caller's own thread, lower overhead but the caller's thread is still the one blocked during the call.
• Thread-pool-based - runs each call on a dedicated, size-bounded thread pool, giving true isolation (the caller's own thread returns immediately) at the cost of extra context-switching overhead.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does Bulkhead solve?Prevents one failing/slow dependency from exhausting shared resources needed by calls to other, healthy dependencies
Where does the name "Bulkhead" come from?A ship's watertight compartments, which stop one flooded section from sinking the whole vessel
Semaphore vs thread-pool bulkhead?Semaphore limits concurrent calls on the caller's own thread (lighter); thread-pool isolates calls onto a dedicated pool (stronger isolation, more overhead)
How does Bulkhead relate to Circuit Breaker?They're complementary - Bulkhead limits how much of a resource one dependency can consume, Circuit Breaker stops calling a dependency altogether once it's clearly unhealthy

beginner.content:
What is Rate Limiting?

Rate Limiting controls HOW MANY requests a client (or a service) is allowed to make in a given time window, protecting a service from being overwhelmed - whether by a buggy retry loop, a traffic spike, or a malicious client.

The Token Bucket Concept

A common algorithm: imagine a bucket that holds up to N tokens, refilled at a steady rate (e.g. 10 tokens/second). Every incoming request must take one token to proceed; if the bucket is empty, the request is rejected (or queued) until a token is available. This allows short bursts (up to the bucket size) while still enforcing a steady average rate.
Resilience4j Rate Limiter Example

expert.content:
Where to Apply Rate Limiting


• At the API Gateway - protects ALL backend services from any single client at once, the most common production placement.
• Per-service - a service protects itself directly, useful when it's called by internal services that bypass the gateway.
• Per-user/API-key - a fairer scheme than a single global limit, so one noisy client can't starve everyone else's quota.

A rate-limited client typically receives an HTTP 429 Too Many Requests status, often with a Retry-After header telling it when it's safe to try again.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does Rate Limiting solve?Protects a service from being overwhelmed by too many requests from one client, whether accidental or malicious
Explain the token bucket algorithmA bucket holds up to N tokens refilled at a steady rate; each request consumes one token, allowing bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing a steady average rate
What HTTP status usually signals a rate-limited request?429 Too Many Requests, often with a Retry-After header
Why rate-limit per-user instead of one global limit?A global limit lets one noisy client starve everyone else's share of the quota

beginner.content:
What is Load Balancing?

When a service has multiple running instances (for scale and redundancy), Load Balancing decides WHICH instance handles each incoming request, spreading traffic evenly so no single instance is overwhelmed while others sit idle.

Client-Side vs Server-Side Load Balancing


• Server-Side - a dedicated load balancer (NGINX, AWS ELB, a Kubernetes Service) sits in front of the instances and routes each request; the caller doesn't know or care which instance handled it.
• Client-Side - the calling service itself fetches the list of healthy instances (often from a service registry, see Service Discovery) and picks one directly, skipping an extra network hop through a middle-man balancer.

Common Balancing Strategies


• Round Robin - cycles through instances in order, simple and fair when instances are similarly sized.
• Least Connections - sends the next request to whichever instance currently has the fewest active connections, better when requests vary a lot in duration.
• Weighted - larger/more powerful instances get proportionally more traffic.
• Random - picks an instance at random, surprisingly effective at scale and very cheap to compute.

expert.content:
Health-Aware Load Balancing

A good load balancer doesn't just spread traffic evenly - it also stops sending traffic to instances failing health checks, removing them from rotation until they recover. Combined with Service Discovery's heartbeat mechanism, this is how a whole unhealthy instance gets naturally drained of traffic without any manual intervention.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Client-side vs server-side load balancing?Server-side: a dedicated balancer routes traffic, caller is unaware of instances. Client-side: the caller itself picks an instance from the registry, skipping the extra hop
Round Robin vs Least Connections?Round Robin cycles through instances in order (simple, fair for similar workloads); Least Connections favors the instance with fewest active connections (better for uneven request durations)
How does load balancing interact with health checks?Unhealthy instances get removed from the rotation automatically, so traffic naturally drains away from them without manual action

beginner.content:
The Problem

A traditional single-database transaction (BEGIN...COMMIT/ROLLBACK) guarantees all-or-nothing across multiple table writes. But in microservices, "place an order" might span Order Service, Payment Service, and Inventory Service - each with its OWN database. There is no single database transaction that can atomically span all three.

What is the Saga Pattern?

A Saga breaks a distributed transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each in one service, with each step publishing an event/message that triggers the next step. If a step fails partway through, the Saga runs compensating transactions to undo the effects of the steps that already succeeded - rather than a true rollback (which isn't possible across services).

Choreography vs Orchestration


• Choreography - each service listens for events and reacts on its own, publishing its own events in turn; there's no central coordinator. Simple for short sagas, but the overall flow becomes hard to see/trace as more steps get added.
• Orchestration - a central Saga Orchestrator explicitly tells each service what to do next and handles compensation logic itself. Easier to understand/debug for complex flows, at the cost of a new central component.

expert.content:
Compensating Transactions Are Not True Rollbacks

A compensating transaction UNDOES the business effect of a prior step, but it can't always erase every side effect (e.g. a "cancel order" email may already have been sent, or a "sorry, order cancelled" notification is itself a new, visible action, not silence). Sagas must be designed with this in mind - compensation is "make it right going forward," not "pretend it never happened."

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why can't microservices use a normal ACID transaction across services?Each service owns its own database; there's no single transaction manager that can span multiple independent databases atomically
What is a compensating transaction?A step that undoes the business effect of an earlier completed step in the saga, run when a later step fails
Choreography vs Orchestration Saga?Choreography: services react to each other's events with no central coordinator. Orchestration: a central orchestrator explicitly directs each step and compensation
What's a downside of choreography as a saga grows?The overall flow becomes hard to trace/understand since logic is scattered across many independent event listeners

beginner.content:
What is CQRS?

CQRS separates the model used to WRITE data (Commands - "place this order," "update this profile") from the model used to READ data (Queries - "show me this order's status"), instead of using one single model for both.

Why Separate Them?


• Read and write workloads often have very different needs - reads are usually much more frequent and can tolerate slightly-stale data; writes need strict consistency.
• The optimal data shape for writing (normalized, transactional) is often NOT the optimal shape for reading (denormalized, pre-joined, fast to query).
• They can be scaled independently - e.g. many read replicas for a read-heavy system, without touching the write path at all.
A Simple CQRS Split

expert.content:
Eventual Consistency Between the Two Sides

When the write and read models are physically separate stores, the read side is updated asynchronously (often via the events published on write) - meaning there's a small window where a just-written change hasn't reached the read model yet. CQRS deliberately trades strict immediate consistency for read-side scalability/performance, so systems adopting it must be comfortable with that trade-off for the specific use case.

CQRS is frequently paired with Event Sourcing (see that separate topic) since events are a natural way to propagate write-side changes into the read model, but the two patterns are independent - you can use CQRS without Event Sourcing.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does CQRS stand for and mean?Command Query Responsibility Segregation - separating the write model (Commands) from the read model (Queries)
Why might the ideal write schema differ from the ideal read schema?Writes favor a normalized, transactionally-consistent shape; reads favor a denormalized, pre-joined shape optimized for fast queries
What consistency trade-off does CQRS usually introduce?Eventual consistency - the read model lags slightly behind the write model since it's updated asynchronously
Is CQRS the same thing as Event Sourcing?No - they're often paired together but are independent patterns; CQRS can be used without Event Sourcing

beginner.content:
What is Event Sourcing?

Event Sourcing is a pattern where, instead of storing just the current state of an entity in a database, you store the full sequence of immutable events that led to that state. The current state is derived by replaying those events from the beginning (or from a snapshot).

Traditional Storage vs Event Sourcing


• Traditional (CRUD): A row is updated in place - the history of how it got there is lost.
• Event Sourcing: Every change (OrderCreated, OrderPaid, OrderShipped) is appended as an event - the current state is a "projection" computed from all events.

Why Use Event Sourcing?


• Full audit trail - every state change is recorded, nothing is ever silently overwritten.
• Temporal queries - you can reconstruct what the state looked like at any point in time by replaying events up to that point.
• Natural fit with event-driven microservices - the events that changed state are exactly what other services want to react to.

expert.content:
Costs and Snapshots

Event Sourcing isn't free:

• Complexity - querying "current state" requires replaying events (or maintaining a separate read model, see CQRS), which is more work than a simple SELECT.
• Eventual consistency - if projections are built asynchronously, readers may briefly see stale state.
• Event schema evolution - old events must remain readable/interpretable even as the event schema evolves over years.

Snapshots

For an entity with thousands of events, replaying all of them on every read is slow. A snapshot periodically saves the computed state at a point in time, so replay only needs to start from the last snapshot plus the events after it - not from the beginning.

Event Sourcing pairs naturally with CQRS (separate read/write models) since the event stream is the write model, and one or more projections built from it serve as read models.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does Event Sourcing store, instead of current state?An append-only, immutable sequence of events describing every change that ever happened
How is "current state" obtained?By replaying all events for that entity (optionally starting from a saved snapshot)
What is a snapshot used for?To avoid replaying an entity's entire event history on every read, by periodically caching a computed state
What pattern does Event Sourcing commonly pair with?CQRS - the event stream serves as the write model, separate projections serve as read models

beginner.content:
What is the Strangler Fig Pattern?

Named after the strangler fig vine, which grows around a host tree and gradually replaces it - the Strangler Fig Pattern is a strategy for incrementally migrating a legacy monolith to microservices without a risky "big bang" rewrite.

How It Works


Step 1: Client --> [Facade/Router] --> Legacy Monolith (handles everything)

Step 2: Client --> [Facade/Router] --> New "Orders" microservice (feature migrated)
                          |
                          --> Legacy Monolith (handles everything else)

Step 3 (repeat per feature)... until:

Step N: Client --> [Facade/Router] --> All traffic now goes to new microservices
                                        Legacy Monolith retired
A routing layer (often the API Gateway) sits in front of both systems and directs each request to either the new microservice (if that feature has been migrated) or the old monolith (if it hasn't yet). Feature by feature, traffic is "strangled" away from the monolith until nothing depends on it and it can be safely decommissioned.

Why Not Just Rewrite Everything at Once?


• A big-bang rewrite risks a long period with no new features shipping, and a single high-stakes cutover where anything can go wrong.
• Strangler Fig lets you migrate and validate one feature at a time, with the old system as a safety net throughout.

expert.content:
Practical Considerations

• Data synchronization - during the transition, both the legacy system and new services may need access to the same data, requiring careful synchronization or a shared database temporarily.
• Routing rules get complex - as more features migrate, the router's rules (by URL path, by feature flag, by user segment) need careful management.
• Know when to stop - some legacy functionality may never be worth migrating; the goal is de-risking migration, not migrating 100% of everything unconditionally.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does Strangler Fig solve?The risk of a single, all-at-once "big bang" rewrite when migrating a legacy system to microservices
What component typically does the routing?A facade or API Gateway that directs each request to the new service (if migrated) or the legacy monolith (if not)
What's a key risk during the transition period?Keeping data consistent between the legacy system and new services while both are still partially in use

beginner.content:
What is the Sidecar Pattern?

The Sidecar Pattern deploys a helper component alongside a main service - in the same deployment unit (same pod in Kubernetes, or same host) - to handle cross-cutting concerns like logging, monitoring, proxying, or security, without modifying the main service's own code.

Just like a motorcycle sidecar travels attached to the motorcycle, sharing its journey but staying a separate compartment, a sidecar container runs next to the main application container, sharing its lifecycle (deployed/scaled/removed together) but staying independently deployable/upgradable.

Common Sidecar Responsibilities


• Network proxying - intercepting inbound/outbound traffic (this is exactly how a service mesh's data plane works).
• Logging/metrics collection - shipping logs or metrics off the main container without the app needing a logging library baked in.
• Configuration/secrets fetching - pulling config or secrets and exposing them locally to the main app.
• TLS termination - handling encryption so the main service can speak plain HTTP internally.

expert.content:
Sidecar and Service Mesh

The most common real-world use of the Sidecar Pattern today is as the data plane of a service mesh (e.g. Istio with the Envoy proxy). Every service gets an Envoy sidecar; all inbound/outbound traffic passes through it, so the mesh can uniformly apply retries, circuit breaking, mTLS, and observability - without any of that logic living in the application code itself.

Trade-offs


• Added latency - every network hop now goes through an extra proxy.
• Added resource overhead - each pod runs (at least) two containers instead of one.
• Operational complexity - sidecars themselves need to be deployed, versioned, and monitored.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a sidecar, structurally?A helper container/process deployed alongside the main service, sharing its lifecycle but running as a separate process
What's the most common production use of the Sidecar Pattern?As the data-plane proxy (e.g. Envoy) in a service mesh, handling traffic/security/observability uniformly across services
What's a downside of the Sidecar Pattern?Extra latency (one more network hop) and extra resource overhead (an additional container per instance)

beginner.content:
What is the Aggregator Pattern?

In a microservices architecture, a single client-facing feature often needs data from multiple backend services. The Aggregator Pattern introduces a dedicated component that calls those services (often in parallel), combines their responses, and returns one unified result to the client - so the client doesn't need to know about or call multiple services itself.

Example: A Product Page

A product detail page might need: product info from a Catalog service, price/discounts from a Pricing service, and stock levels from an Inventory service. Without an aggregator, the client (a mobile app, say) would need to make 3 separate calls and stitch the results together itself.

expert.content:
Where the Aggregator Lives

The aggregator can be implemented as: a dedicated "aggregator service", logic inside an API Gateway, or a Backend for Frontend (BFF) tailored to one client type. Calling downstream services in parallel (rather than sequentially) is usually critical for acceptable latency - the aggregator's total response time is roughly the slowest single downstream call, not the sum of all of them.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does the Aggregator Pattern solve?Avoiding forcing the client to call multiple backend services itself and stitch together the results
Why call downstream services in parallel rather than sequentially?So total latency is close to the slowest single call, instead of the sum of all calls
Where is an aggregator commonly implemented?As a dedicated aggregator service, inside an API Gateway, or as part of a Backend for Frontend (BFF)

beginner.content:
What is the Backend for Frontend (BFF) Pattern?

Different client types (a web app, an iOS app, an Android app) often have very different needs - different data shapes, different amounts of data (a mobile app wants a lean payload, a web dashboard wants everything), different interaction patterns. The BFF Pattern gives each client type its own dedicated backend, tailored specifically to that client, instead of one generic API trying to satisfy every client equally well (and usually satisfying none of them well).

Without BFF vs With BFF


• Without BFF: One shared API serves web, mobile, and third-party partners - it either over-fetches for mobile or under-fetches for web, and any client-specific change risks breaking other clients.
• With BFF: Each client talks to its own BFF (Web BFF, Mobile BFF), which in turn calls the shared backend microservices and shapes the response specifically for that client.

expert.content:
Trade-offs

• Benefit: each client team can evolve its BFF independently, optimized exactly for that client's needs, without waiting on or breaking other clients.
• Cost: more services to build, deploy, and maintain - some logic may end up duplicated across BFFs unless carefully factored into shared libraries or the underlying microservices.

BFF is essentially a specialized case of the Aggregator Pattern - a BFF is an aggregator, just one scoped and owned per client type rather than shared generically.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer

beginner.content:
What is Event-Driven Communication?

Instead of Service A calling Service B directly (synchronous request/response), Event-Driven Communication has Service A publish an event ("OrderPlaced") to a broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ), and any number of interested services subscribe to and react to that event independently. The producer doesn't know or care who (if anyone) is listening.

Synchronous (Direct Call) vs Event-Driven


• Synchronous: Order service directly calls Inventory service, Payment service, Notification service - one by one, waiting for each - tightly coupled, and if one is down, the whole flow can fail.
• Event-Driven: Order service publishes "OrderPlaced" once - Inventory, Payment, and Notification services each independently subscribe and react whenever they're ready. Adding a new subscriber later requires zero changes to the Order service.

expert.content:
Benefits and Trade-offs

• Loose coupling - producers and consumers don't know about each other, only about the event/broker.
• Independent scaling and failure isolation - a slow or down consumer doesn't block the producer.
• Trade-off: eventual consistency - there's a delay between an event being published and all consumers processing it; the system is not instantly consistent everywhere.
• Trade-off: harder to trace - following a business flow across many independently-reacting consumers needs good distributed tracing/observability.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer

What's the main trade-off of going event-driven?Eventual consistency - consumers process events with some delay rather than the system being instantly consistent everywhere
Why is event-driven communication good for adding new features?A new consumer can subscribe to an existing event stream without requiring any change to the producer

beginner.content:
The Dual-Write Problem

Imagine a service that, in one operation, needs to (1) save an order to its database AND (2) publish an "OrderPlaced" event to a message broker. These are two separate systems - if the database write succeeds but publishing the event fails (network blip, broker down), the order exists but nobody was ever notified. This inconsistency is the dual-write problem.

What is the Outbox Pattern?

The Outbox Pattern solves this by writing the event into an "outbox" table in the SAME database transaction as the business data change - so either both are saved together, or neither is (standard single-database transaction guarantees). A separate process then reads unpublished rows from the outbox table and publishes them to the broker, marking them as sent.

Single DB Transaction:
  1. INSERT INTO orders (...)
  2. INSERT INTO outbox (event_type, payload, sent=false)
  COMMIT  <-- both rows saved together, or neither is

Separate Relay Process:
  SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE sent = false
  -> publish each to Kafka/RabbitMQ
  -> UPDATE outbox SET sent = true

expert.content:
How the Relay Reads the Outbox

Two common approaches for the relay process:

• Polling publisher - a background job periodically queries the outbox table for unsent rows and publishes them.
• Change Data Capture (CDC) - a tool like Debezium tails the database's write-ahead log/binlog and streams new outbox rows to the broker automatically, with lower latency than polling.

The outbox table itself typically gets cleaned up (rows deleted or archived) after successful publishing, so it doesn't grow unbounded.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the dual-write problem?When a service must atomically update its database AND publish a message, but these are two separate systems that can't share one transaction, risking inconsistency if one succeeds and the other fails
How does the Outbox Pattern solve it?By writing the event into an outbox table in the SAME local database transaction as the business change, then a separate relay process publishes from the outbox to the broker
What's a common way to implement the relay process?Either a polling job that queries unsent outbox rows, or Change Data Capture (e.g. Debezium) tailing the database log

beginner.content:
What is a Distributed Lock?

A regular Java synchronized block or ReentrantLock only coordinates threads within a single JVM process. When multiple separate service instances (potentially on different machines) need exclusive access to a shared resource - like ensuring only one instance processes a given scheduled job, or only one instance updates a shared record at a time - you need a distributed lock: a lock that's visible and enforced across process/machine boundaries, typically implemented using a shared external system like Redis, ZooKeeper, or the database itself.

A Simple Redis-Based Lock (Conceptual)


SET lock:job-123 my-instance-id NX PX 30000
  NX  -> only set if the key doesn't already exist (acquire only if free)
  PX 30000 -> auto-expire after 30 seconds (safety net if the holder crashes)

... do the exclusive work ...

DEL lock:job-123   (release the lock, only if we still own it)

expert.content:
The Hard Part: Correctness Under Failure

Distributed locks are notoriously easy to get subtly wrong:

• Clock skew - lock expiry times rely on clocks; if a node's clock is off, it might believe it still holds a lock that has actually expired elsewhere.
• "Still running but lock expired" race - if the lock auto-expires (as a crash safety net) while the original holder is still slow-but-alive, ANOTHER process can now acquire the lock, and you end up with two processes both believing they hold exclusive access.
• Redlock debate - Redis's official multi-node "Redlock" algorithm for stronger distributed-lock guarantees is genuinely contested in the distributed-systems community (notably criticized by Martin Kleppmann) for not being safe under certain failure/GC-pause scenarios - know that this is a real, debated trade-off, not a solved problem.
• Fencing tokens - a mitigation: the lock issues a monotonically increasing token on each acquisition; the protected resource rejects any write carrying an older token than the last one it saw, protecting against a "zombie" holder that thinks it still owns the lock.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why can't a plain Java ReentrantLock coordinate across service instances?It only exists within one JVM process's memory - separate instances (possibly on different machines) have no visibility into it
Why does a distributed lock usually have an expiry/TTL?As a safety net so the lock is eventually released automatically if the holder crashes without releasing it, preventing a permanent deadlock
What risk does a TTL-based lock introduce?If the holder is still working but slow, the lock can expire and be acquired by another process too early, causing two processes to believe they have exclusive access
What is a fencing token?A monotonically increasing number issued on each lock acquisition, used by the protected resource to reject stale writes from a process that no longer actually holds the lock

beginner.content:
What Does Idempotent Mean?

An operation is idempotent if calling it once has the exact same effect as calling it multiple times. This matters enormously in distributed systems because retries are unavoidable - a client may not know whether its request actually reached the server (the response was lost, not the request), so it retries "just in case" - and if the original request DID succeed, that retry must not cause a duplicate effect (e.g. charging a customer twice).

Naturally Idempotent vs Not


• Idempotent by nature: setBalance(100) - calling it 5 times still leaves the balance at exactly 100.
• NOT idempotent by nature: addToBalance(100) - calling it 5 times adds 500, not 100. A retried "add 100" could silently overcharge or overcredit.

Idempotency Keys

The standard fix for a non-naturally-idempotent operation (like "place an order" or "charge a card") is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique key per logical request (e.g. a UUID) and sends it with every attempt (including retries). The server remembers which keys it has already processed and, on seeing a repeated key, returns the SAME result as before instead of performing the operation again.

expert.content:
Where Idempotency Matters in Microservices

• Payment/order APIs - the classic case; a lost response must never mean "charge twice".
• Message consumers - most message brokers offer "at-least-once" delivery, meaning a consumer MUST be written to handle receiving the same message more than once without double-processing it.
• Retry logic (see the Retry Pattern) - retries are only safe to apply automatically/transparently when the underlying operation is idempotent; otherwise a well-intentioned retry can cause real harm.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does "idempotent" mean for an operation?Calling it once has the same effect as calling it multiple times
Why does idempotency matter for retries?Because a client can't always tell whether a failed-looking request actually succeeded server-side, so it must retry - and that retry must not double-apply the effect
What is an idempotency key?A unique key the client attaches to every attempt of the same logical request, letting the server recognize and safely no-op a retry instead of repeating the operation
Give an example of an operation that is NOT naturally idempotent.addToBalance(100) / incrementing a counter - repeating it changes the result each time, unlike setBalance(100) which is naturally idempotent

cheatNotes: API Gateway - single entry point for routing, auth, and rate limiting across microservices
Service Discovery - dynamic lookup of service instance locations via a registry (Eureka/Consul)
Circuit Breaker - trips OPEN after repeated failures to stop cascading failure, tests recovery via HALF-OPEN
Retry - re-attempts transient failures with exponential backoff + jitter to avoid retry storms
Timeout - bounds how long a caller waits, preventing indefinite resource pileup
Bulkhead - isolates resources per dependency so one failure can't exhaust resources needed by others
Rate Limiting - caps requests per time window (token bucket), returns HTTP 429 when exceeded
Saga - sequence of local transactions with compensating actions, since no cross-service ACID transaction exists
CQRS - separates the write model from the read model to optimize/scale each independently
